title: She Is More Righteous Than I — Going Down, a Veil, Recognition
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. The chapter in front of us today is one that a great many Bible reading plans quietly step around. Its content is hard to preach; from the pulpit it has to be clear, and it has to be restrained. So let me say at the outset what we are doing: today we are not chasing the details. We are chasing six words.

Let me start by putting a question to you. Is there something in your life where the very same behaviour, when it happens in you, gets called "understandable, given the circumstances", and when it happens in somebody else gets called "unforgivable"?

In Genesis 38 Judah does something at the side of a road, and afterwards he says, "Let her keep it, lest we be shamed." Three months later somebody tells him that his daughter-in-law is pregnant, and he says, "Bring her out, and let her be burned!"

And then that woman sends him three objects: a signet, a cord, a staff. She says, "Please discern whose these are." Judah answers with six words, and those six words rewrote the whole second half of his life: "She is more righteous than I."
1. He Went Down from His Brothers
"At that time, Judah went down from his brothers, and visited a certain Adullamite, whose name was Hirah." (Genesis 38:1)

"At that time" — the Hebrew is בָּעֵת הַהִוא (*ba'et hahi*), and it fastens this chapter directly onto the one before it. In that chapter Judah had said one sentence: "What profit is it if we kill our brother …? Come, and let's sell him." Twenty pieces of silver, and a younger brother was sold.
And then the first verb of this chapter is "went down" — יָרַד (*yarad*). Down from the hill country of Hebron into the lowland of Adullam.

Brothers and sisters, "up" and "down" in the Bible are very often more than geography. Joseph is sold and taken "down" into Egypt; Judah is going "down" too, on his own two feet. A man pushes his younger brother down into a pit, and then he himself begins to walk downhill.

And what he does next is three things that his father and his grandfather had both been expressly forbidden to do: he leaves his brothers, he marries the daughter of a Canaanite man, and he settles his household there. In chapter 24 Abraham gave the charge; in chapter 28 Isaac gave the charge: no wife from the daughters of Canaan.

The commonest route sin takes is not one leap off a cliff. It is a long slope downhill. He left, he turned aside, he settled — three thoroughly ordinary verbs inside a single verse, and between them they have carried a man clean out of the land of promise.

What happens next the text writes at speed. Of the firstborn, Er, it says he "was wicked in Yahweh's sight. So Yahweh killed him." The second son, Onan, would not raise up offspring for his brother, and "the thing which he did was evil in Yahweh's sight, and he killed him also."
Then Judah says to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, "Remain a widow in your father's house, until Shelah, my son, is grown up."
The second half of verse 11 is the first key to the whole chapter: "for he said, 'Lest he also die, like his brothers.'"
His mouth says "wait." His heart says "never." He has taken the deaths of his two sons and charged them to this woman's account.

"Until my son is grown up" — a wait with no date attached to it is simply a refusal with good manners on. Brothers and sisters, we are experts at this ourselves: "we'll talk about it later", "when I have some time", "when the moment comes I'll deal with it." Nothing in those sentences is untrue. But that word "lest" down in the heart — we know quite well that it is there.

And Tamar? She puts on the garments of her widowhood, goes back to her father's house, and waits, one year after another. The text says "after many days" — and the Hebrew behind it is "the days multiplied." We are never told how many years. All she knows is that Shelah has grown up, and nobody has come for her.
Joseph's story is only half told. Why is a chapter about Judah shoved into the middle of it?

It is not in the wrong place; it is a deliberate comparison. In the previous chapter Judah said, "What profit is it if we kill our brother …? Come, and let's sell him," and a brother went for twenty pieces of silver. The very first verb of this chapter is "went down" — down from the hill country of Hebron into the lowland of Adullam. Joseph is sold and taken down into Egypt; Judah is going down under his own power. The text sets the two men side by side: one is sold into a foreign country and stands, the other is free in his own homeland and slides. And what matters even more is the ending — the branch that grows out of the close of this chapter is the very line of the Messiah's genealogy. The way God chooses is very often not our order of things.
Left, turned aside, settled — why should we stop and look at those three verbs?

Because the commonest route sin takes is not one leap off a cliff; it is a long slope downhill. Three thoroughly ordinary verbs inside the first verse are enough to carry a man out of the land of promise: he left his brothers, he turned aside to an Adullamite's house, and he settled his household there. And what he does next is precisely what his father and his grandfather were both expressly forbidden to do — in chapter 24 Abraham gave the charge, in chapter 28 Isaac gave the charge: no wife from the daughters of Canaan. So the thing to guard against is not the great catastrophe. It is those three small movements. In practice you can ask yourself three questions: which group of people have I lately left? Where have I moved my time to? And where have I settled down?
"Until Shelah, my son, is grown up" — what exactly is wrong with that sentence?

What is wrong with it is the second half of verse 11: "for he said, 'Lest he also die, like his brothers.'" His mouth says "wait"; his heart says "never" — and he has charged the deaths of his two sons to this woman's account. A wait with no date attached is a refusal with good manners on. We are very good at this too: "we'll talk about it later", "when I have some time", "when the moment comes I'll deal with it." Nothing in those sentences is untrue, but that "lest" down in the heart — we know it is there. The practical test is simple. If you do not intend to do it, say no honestly. Stringing a person along on a date that will never arrive wounds more than a refusal does.
2. A Light from the Original: a Drama of Mistaken Identity
Verse 12: Judah's wife dies, he "was comforted", and he goes up to Timnah to his sheep shearers.

"Was comforted" is וַיִּנָּחֶם (*vayinnachem*). In the chapter before, Jacob said, "For I will go down to Sheol to my son, mourning," and the text says of him that "he refused to be comforted" — the same Hebrew root. One father would not be comforted; the other father was comforted soon enough. The text has deliberately set these two men next to each other.
Sheep shearing was a festival season in the ancient Near East — harvest, feasting, and a time when a man's restraint comes off very easily.
Tamar hears about it. She "took off the garments of her widowhood, and covered herself with her veil", and sits down in the gateway of a town on the road up to Timnah.
The name of that place is Enaim, עֵינַיִם (*Enayim*), and it means, literally, "two eyes", "the opening of the eyes."
And then the text says, "When Judah saw her, he thought that she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face." (Genesis 38:15)
"He thought" — from beginning to end this chapter is a drama of mistaken identity. He is standing at the Gate of Two Eyes, and his eyes do not recognise who is in front of him.
What happens next the text records with great restraint, and we shall leave it there too. What I want you to notice is three objects: the signet, the cord, the staff.

The "signet" (חוֹתָם, *chotam*) was a man's proof of identity in the ancient world, the equivalent of a signature today; the "cord" was the string the seal hung from; and the "staff" (מַטֶּה, *matteh*) was the emblem of standing and authority — the same word later comes to mean "tribe."
Which is to say: he pawned his identity papers, his personal seal and his authority — all of it — to a stranger at the side of a road.

And the word for "pledge" is עֵרָבוֹן (*erabon*). Carried over into Greek, that word became the New Testament's ἀρραβών — it is the very word Paul is using when he says the Holy Spirit "is a pledge of our inheritance." One and the same word: on one side a token handed over as security, on the other side God's own guarantee given to us.
Verse 20: Judah sends the young goat by the hand of his friend, to redeem the pledge. Notice that he does not go himself — this kind of errand gets handed to somebody else.
And then that passage says it three times over: "he didn't find her", "I haven't found her", "you haven't found her."
And the answer of the local men comes twice over: "There has been no prostitute here."
So Judah says, "Let her keep it, lest we be shamed." (Genesis 38:23)
Listen carefully to what he actually cares about. Not the three tokens. Not the woman. "Lest we be shamed" — what other people will think of him.

Brothers and sisters, before a man is caught, what he cares about most is very often not right and wrong but face. And that thing called face is what will make a man, three months later, say something truly terrible.
The signet, the cord and the staff — how much weight do those three carry?

The "signet" was a man's proof of identity in the ancient world, the equivalent of a signature today; the "cord" was the string the seal hung from; and the "staff" was the emblem of standing and authority, the same word that later comes to mean "tribe." Which is to say: he pawned his identity papers, his seal and his authority, the lot, to a stranger at the side of a road. And the word for "pledge" here is עֵרָבוֹן (*erabon*); carried over into Greek it became the New Testament's ἀρραβών — the very word Paul uses when he says the Holy Spirit "is a pledge of our inheritance." One and the same word: on one side the token a man hands over in a moment when his restraint is off, on the other side God's own guarantee to us. And the incident is a warning all by itself: when a person lets himself go, the first thing he pawns is usually his own identity.
"Let her keep it, lest we be shamed" — what does that sentence give away?

It gives away what he actually cares about. Not the three tokens, not the woman — "lest we be shamed." What other people will think of him. And notice as well that when the young goat went off to redeem the pledge, he did not go himself; this kind of errand gets handed to somebody else. Before a person is caught, what he cares about most is very often not right and wrong but face. That is worth holding up against our own day: a great many wrongs go unaddressed not because the conscience is missing but because being found out is unbearable. And a man who is afraid of being found out will usually work all the harder at accusing other people — which is precisely why, three months later, he says the terrible thing he says.
3. Bring Her Out, and Let Her Be Burned

"About three months later, Judah was told, 'Tamar, your daughter-in-law, has played the prostitute. Moreover, behold, she is with child by prostitution.' Judah said, 'Bring her out, and let her be burned.'" (Genesis 38:24)

First: "Judah was told" — the Hebrew is a passive, וַיֻּגַּד (*vayyuggad*). In the chapter before, his brothers likewise sent the coat along and "brought it to their father", letting somebody else do the speaking. The same technique — and this time it is his turn to be the one who gets told.
Second, and this is the part that stings the eye: the same act. When he does it, it is "let her keep it." When somebody else does it, it is "let her be burned."
And the sentence is out of all proportion. Burning was among the gravest penalties in the law of that time, and a case of this kind would not ordinarily have been pushed anywhere near that far.
Brothers and sisters, this is the definition of a double standard: the same act — when I do it, it is called a difficulty; when you do it, it is called sin.

And I must warn you of something more frightening still. When a person is carrying a debt in his own heart, he is often especially savage towards other people. That is not righteous anger; that is cover. Set the fire burning on somebody else, and you never have to look at the fire burning in yourself.

"When she was brought out, she sent to her father-in-law, saying, 'I am with child by the man who owns these.' She also said, 'Please discern whose these are — the signet, and the cords, and the staff.'" (Genesis 38:25)

"Please discern" is הַכֶּר־נָא (*haker-na*) in the Hebrew — and it is word for word the same phrase the sons used in the chapter before, when they brought the blood-soaked coat to Jacob and said, "Examine it, now." The English renders the two places differently; in the Hebrew they are identical.
In the previous chapter, Judah was the man holding the evidence and asking his father to identify it. In this chapter, he has become the man who is asked to identify.

And look at the way she does it. She does not shout his name out in front of everybody. She sends the evidence to him and lets him decide for himself whether he will own it. She is being dragged out to be burned alive, and she still leaves him a way to keep his dignity.
And then comes the summit of the chapter, which is also the reason the chapter exists at all:
"Judah acknowledged them, and said, 'She is more righteous than I, because I didn't give her to Shelah, my son.' He knew her again no more." (Genesis 38:26)

"Acknowledged" is וַיַּכֵּר (*vayyaker*) — the same verb used in the chapter before when Jacob "recognized" the coat. And "she is more righteous than I" is צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי (*tzadkah mimmenni*) — this is the only time in the whole Old Testament that a man says such a thing about a woman.
Brothers and sisters, notice three features of this confession.
First, he does not explain. He does not say, "the situation at the time was such and such." He does not say, "she was in the wrong as well."
Second, he names his own item: "because I didn't give her to Shelah, my son." What he owns is not that one night. It is that one promise he never made good on — and that is the root of the thing.
Third, and most important of all: "He knew her again no more." He stopped.

Real repentance is two things happening together: you own it, and then you stop. Owning it without stopping is emotion. Stopping without owning it is suppression. Both together — that is what repentance is.
And this one confession saved two lives on the spot: Tamar's, and the life of the child in her womb. One true sentence can save a person.
The same act: "let her keep it" when he does it, "let her be burned" when someone else does it. What is going on there?

That is the definition of a double standard: the same act — when I do it, it is called a difficulty; when you do it, it is called sin. And the sentence is plainly out of proportion — burning was among the gravest penalties in the law of that time, and a case like this would not ordinarily have been pushed that far. There is something still more frightening to be said here: when a person is carrying a debt in his own heart, he is often especially savage towards other people. That is not righteous anger; that is cover. Set the fire on somebody else and you never have to see the fire in yourself. So when you find there is a particular kind of person you simply cannot tolerate, it is worth stopping to ask one question: is there something of the very same sort in me that I have never dealt with?
4. Perez: Grace Comes Out of the Least Presentable Place
The end of this chapter is the birth of a pair of twins.

One of them puts out a hand first, and the midwife ties a scarlet thread on it; and then that hand is drawn back, and the other one comes out first. The midwife says, "Why have you made a breach for yourself?"
"Made a breach" is מַה־פָּרַצְתָּ (*mah-paratzta*) in the Hebrew, literally "how have you burst through?" And so that child is named Perez, פֶּרֶץ (*Peretz*) — a breach, a man who bursts through.

Brothers and sisters, in this family the one who comes later comes out on top yet again. Isaac was not the firstborn. Jacob was not the firstborn. And Perez was not the one who put out his hand first. God's choosing has never followed the order human beings would set.
Then go and read the closing lines of Ruth chapter 4: "Now this is the history of the generations of Perez … and Obed became the father of Jesse, and Jesse became the father of David."
And then go and read Matthew chapter 1, verse 3: "Judah became the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar."
Matthew writes out the genealogy of Jesus Christ, forty-two generations, and he gives the names of only four mothers. Tamar is the first of them.

A biblical author sitting down to write the family line of the Messiah could very easily have set down the fathers' names only, and passed over this chapter in silence. But the Holy Spirit did not let him pass over it. God left this page inside the genealogy of his own Son.

So if there is something in your heart about which you think, "that one is too filthy, God could never use me again" — please open Matthew chapter 1 and read it slowly. God's family register is not a roll of honour. It is an inventory of grace.
And now we can see why this chapter had to be inserted into the middle of Joseph's story.

In chapter 37, Judah is the one who proposes selling his brother. In chapter 38, Judah learns to say, "I was wrong." And by chapter 44, the man who sold a brother for twenty pieces of silver is standing in front of the prime minister of Egypt saying, "Now therefore, please let your servant stay instead of the boy, my lord's slave; and let the boy go up with his brothers."
From "sell the brother" to "trade myself for the brother" — what lies in between is this chapter.
And Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49 says, "Judah is a lion's cub … The scepter will not depart from Judah." And Revelation says, "the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah … has overcome."
That Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah really did make himself a servant in our place.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
This chapter is hard to preach, and there are several places where we have to be particularly careful.

The first distortion is preaching it too explicitly, as a piece of exotica. This chapter contains sensitive material; the pulpit has to be clear, and the pulpit has to be restrained. Preach the details too finely and what the congregation carries out through the door will be the plot, not the confession. The test is very simple: when the meeting breaks up, is it the story they remember, or "she is more righteous than I"?

The second distortion is holding Tamar's tactics up as a model. The text nowhere praises her method; what the text says is that Judah wronged her first. Her situation deserves sympathy; her method is not to be copied. Make a model of it and what the congregation learns is that a person may use tactics to get hold of what is rightfully his.

The third distortion is skipping the chapter as an irrelevant interlude. Those two Hebrew words, "please discern", stitch chapter 37 and chapter 44 together; and Perez walks straight into the genealogy of David and of Christ. Skip it, and you have dropped the hinge on which Judah's whole change turns. Does your congregation understand why this chapter sits exactly where it sits?

The fourth distortion is preaching the sin and never preaching the line of salvation running through it. Out of the least presentable story in the book, God brought David, and God brought Christ. Preach failure alone and the congregation will be left standing inside their shame with no way out of it. The test is this: when someone who thinks his own past is too filthy has heard you, can he see a road?

The fifth distortion is preaching "she is more righteous than I" as though Judah were a good man from that day onward. The text does not say so. It says only that he owned it, and that he stopped. Repentance is a starting point, not a graduation certificate.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: we find it terribly hard to say the words "I was wrong." We will say, "there are things about this that I got wrong too." We will say, "all right, all right, it's all my fault" — that is not owning it, that is closing down the conversation. And more than anything we will say "but": "I'm sorry, but at the time you also …" The moment that "but" is out of the mouth, the sentence in front of it has been cancelled. Brothers and sisters, when Judah said "she is more righteous than I", there was not half a "but" in it. This week, say to one person, once, "I was wrong" — and then close your mouth. No explanation attached, no condition attached, no "but" attached. You will find that there is an enormous freedom living inside those three words.

The second question: we are extremely good at using "when I have some time" and "we'll talk about it later" to handle the things we do not want to face. Judah said, "until Shelah, my son, is grown up" — it sounds like an arrangement, and it is in fact a date that will never arrive. We say to our children, "once this busy stretch is over." We say to our spouse, "let's talk another day." We say to God, "once I am through this patch." That woman sat in the garments of her widowhood and waited for who knows how many years. Brothers and sisters, that matter in your heart that keeps getting "later" — it has a name, and there is a person waiting on it. This week, fix the date.
"Please discern" — what is there to learn from the way Tamar did it?

In the Hebrew those words are הַכֶּר־נָא (*haker-na*), and they are word for word the phrase the sons used in the chapter before, when they put the blood-soaked coat in front of Jacob — the English renders the two places differently, but the Hebrew is identical. In that chapter Judah was the man holding the evidence and asking his father to identify it; in this chapter he becomes the man who is asked to identify. And her way of doing it is very much worth learning. She did not shout his name out in front of the crowd. She sent the evidence to him and let him decide for himself whether to own it — she was being dragged out to be burned alive, and she still left him a way to keep his dignity. You can point out another person's wrong without executing him in the public square; give a man room to admit it himself, and that admission will actually change him.
7. Living 321 Out — Own It, Then Stop
Brothers and sisters, let us take this lesson and tie it back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Judah says later, "please let your servant stay instead of the boy." He goes from being the man who pawns other people to being the man who puts himself up. And the Lion who came out of his own tribe really did make himself a servant for us — "who, existing in the form of God … emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." That is my role model: he pawned nobody else; he put himself up.

The Bible is my standard. My feelings say, "if I say this out loud I am finished." The standard says, "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." Feeling says that owning it is loss. The standard says that owning it is getting something back.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Who was it that made Judah recognise those three objects at that moment? The signet, the cord and the staff were lying in front of him, and he could perfectly well have flatly denied the whole thing — nobody could have proved anything. The light in his heart at that moment was the work of the Holy Spirit. Rely on your intellect and on yourself and you get worry; rely on the heart and on the Holy Spirit and you get joy. When the Holy Spirit shines on a thing, you do not have to argue. You only have to own it.

Let Jesus be King. "She is more righteous than I" — owning it, plus stopping: that is what repentance is. Letting Jesus be King means that when the truth is laid out in the open you stop making a case for yourself; you vacate the judge's seat, and return to our originally intended position as human beings.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. There is not a single person in this chapter who comes out of it with credit. And yet four thousand years later we read it and what we praise is God — because he was able to bring David out of a page like this, and to bring Christ out of it. The glory does not rest on any human being here, not in the smallest degree; and that is exactly why we can rest easy.

Establish God's system. Perez walked into the family register of David, and he walked into Matthew chapter 1. To establish God's system is a work in which grace is brought out of the least presentable place there is. So do not use your own past to set limits on God — the material he builds with has always been more broken than we imagined.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Confession
We come to this chapter carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "I would never do a thing like that." Judah thought so too, right up until those three objects were laid in front of him. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, measuring out other people's sentences — "bring her out, and let her be burned." Humility is returning to our originally intended position as a human being, and admitting that I am made of exactly the same material as the person I have just condemned.

The fearful heart says, "if I own this, I am finished." When Judah owned it, he was the head of the clan and there were people standing all around him. And after he owned it, he was not finished — on the contrary, that is where the second half of his life began. Fear does the sums on the cost. The gospel does the sums on the freedom.

The ashamed heart says, "my past is too filthy; God will never use me again." Please go and read Matthew chapter 1, verse 3. There is a name in that verse that you would have sworn God would never write down. God not only did not delete it; he put it into the family register of his own Son.

The wounded heart says, "I am the one who did the waiting; I am the one who was cheated; nobody ever came for me." Tamar waited a great many years, and nobody spoke up for her. And yet what the whole Bible finally remembers is not Judah's respectability. It is her name. God remembers the one who waits; when he delays, it is not because he has forgotten.
Four kinds of heart, and one confession. And the reason this confession has any power in it is that at Golgotha one who had no sin of his own owned ours in our place.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, towards God. Take one thing you have been making a case for and confess it straight out in prayer. Do not dress it up, do not add the background briefing; say it in one sentence and be done.

Second, towards yourself. Write down your double standard, one sentence is enough: "With the very same ____, when I do it, it gets called ____; when someone else does it, it gets called ____." Write it down, and bring it to God.
Third, towards other people. Say to one person, once, "I was wrong", with no "but" attached. Say it and then stop; do not rush to get an apology back out of him.

Fourth, towards daily living. This week, pass no comment on anybody's past. Not at the dinner table, not in the group chat, not in your own head. Only a week — and you will find yourself walking a great deal lighter.

Fifth, towards your calling. Read Matthew chapter 1 straight through, slowly, and look at the kinds of people God has used. Then ask yourself: what reason have I got left for saying that God cannot use me?

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. Sentence one: there is a chapter in the Bible where the head of a clan shouts "burn her!" — and the evidence turns out to be his own. Sentence two: in front of everybody he said, "she is more righteous than I", and then he stopped doing what he had been doing. Sentence three: what I admire most about him is not that he never sinned; it is that he owned it, and that he stopped.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will keep two standards no longer; what I do and what another person does are the same act.
I declare that I will say the words "I was wrong", with no "but" attached and no explanation attached.
I declare that I will not only own it, I will stop it; because repentance is those two things happening together.
I declare that my past cannot set limits on God; he is able to bring his work out of the least presentable place there is.
This week I am supposed to own something, and I am afraid that the moment I say it I will be ruined. What do I do?

Look first at Judah's six words: "She is more righteous than I." It cost him something to own it — public humiliation, in front of everybody. And yet those six words rewrote the whole second half of his life: in chapter 44 he stands out as surety for Benjamin and says, "Please let your servant stay instead of the boy, my lord's slave." Owning it is not the end; it is where the turn begins. In practice you can do it like this. First, say it once to God. Second, say it once to one person you trust. Third, own only your own part, and do not go around allocating everybody else's share of the blame. And if the matter involves the law, or would injure someone else, talk it over first with a pastor or with a professional about how to take responsibility for it.

At the opening of this chapter a man walks downhill: he leaves his brothers, turns aside into the lowland, and settles there. At the close of this chapter a man walks uphill: he owns it, he stops, and later he is willing to trade himself for his brother.
And the turn in between is only six words: she is more righteous than I.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because every one of us is carrying a list of things we dare not own; and on the cross, the one who really was righteous stood in our place and said: put this account on me. He pawned nobody else; he put himself up. With his own signet, his own pledge and his own authority, he bought us back.

May God bless every one of us this week with the courage to say those three words, and with the strength to stop what needs stopping; may we stop inventing respectable dates for ourselves, and may what is written on our family register be grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — a lesson that never reaches the third transformation has stopped at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if there is time to spare. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be completed at home.

Special reminder for this lesson: this chapter touches on sex and on shame. In leading it, do not chase the details and do not treat it as exotica; keep the focus on the double standard and on owning it. Inside the group, nobody's private affairs are to be discussed by name.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ The same act: when I do it it is called a difficulty, when you do it it is called sin. In which matter have you lately been using two different measures?
2. ★★ "Until my son is grown up" is a wait with no date on it. Why does a well-mannered refusal wound more than a plain no?
3. ★ Left, turned aside, settled — three thoroughly ordinary verbs. Where does the slope downhill usually begin?
4. ★★ Tamar let him own it himself; she never shouted his name in public. When you point out another person's wrong, how can you leave him room?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I would never do a thing like that), fearful (I am afraid of being found out), ashamed (there is one thing I cannot bring myself to say), wounded (I am the one who was left waiting). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "She is more righteous than I." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Which kind of person can you least tolerate? Might that intolerance have something to do with something of your own?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "What I am most afraid of people finding out is …" (you may say no more than "I know what mine is").
9. ★★ This week, to whom will you own what? Say when, and say how.

Leader's reminder: the questions in this section carry high risk. Anyone at all may answer with nothing more than "I know what mine is", without saying what it is. Do not press for details, do not comment, and follow up with him privately after the meeting; where a matter involves the law or would injure another person, help him seek pastoral and professional advice.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, is there a "we'll talk about it later" that ought to be given an answer? Say how you are going to answer it.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your service, on whom have you been using the stricter measure?
12. ★★★ The one-measure practice: this week, whenever you are about to accuse someone, first ask yourself, "have I ever done this myself?" Say which kind of accusation you fall into most easily.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him to put that question to you this week whenever you pass comment on somebody. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a man in the Bible who wanted his daughter-in-law burned for what she had done, and then the evidence was brought to him and it turned out he had a share in it himself. Second, in front of everybody he said, "she is more righteous than I", and he made no case for himself at all. Third, so what I learned is that owning it is not the ruin of you; it is the first step of starting again. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: who it is that you have been using your stricter measure on, and the one thing you are going to own this week. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to give us the honesty to say "she is more righteous than I", and the gentleness to leave a person room when we have to point something out.
